opening.headline: Understand the structure of citations and grounding functions that link sources to answers, and determine that citations are not a guarantee of accuracy.
body: According to these terms and conditions, the answer is that refunds are made within 7 days, but what if the user tries to find the supporting sentence but cannot tell where it is in the original text? An answer without a source is difficult to believe even if it is correct, and difficult to recognize even if it is wrong.

In this class, we will look at how Claude's Citations, the search_result block that delivers custom search results, and Gemini's Grounding with Google Search connect answers and original text. Next, we look at examples of how citations can lead to misunderstandings when the source document itself is incorrect, and we summarize the standards for establishing a source policy appropriate for the service.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Citation and grounding functions can explain the structure linking answers and sources.
Can read citation blocks and interpret the location of supporting documents
You can analyze the risks that arise when the underlying documents are incorrect and evaluate the source policy.

screens.title: Unable to confirm the source of the answer
screens.lead: First, read the scene below to see what unsourced answers look like to users. As you read, think about ways to connect your answers to the original text.

visual.alt: A scene where the answer bubble without source indication is not connected to the original terms and conditions.
labels: According to these terms and conditions, refunds are due within 7 days
Which sentence does it come from?

paragraphs: The customer support chatbot responded: According to these terms and conditions, refunds are due within 7 days. Users want to check these words and open the full terms and conditions, but it is difficult to find the underlying sentences in the dozens of pages of text. This is because there is no indication of which document and location the answer came from.

Answers without sources create two problems. Even if the answer is right, it's hard to believe, and even if it's wrong, it's hard to notice. This means that neither the user nor the developer operating the service has any clue to verify the answer.

So, we need a function that attaches the original text location to each claim in the answer. The question we will cover in this lesson is how to connect the answer to the original text. We also look at the extent to which that connection is guaranteed.

callout.label: question of the day
callout.text: How can I link the answer to the original text? If there is a connection, can we trust that the answer is correct?

screens.outro: First, let's think about the services that require a source.

screens.title: Services that require attribution
screens.lead: Are there any services that require a source to be added to the answer? When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: What are the areas where getting it wrong is costly?
items.answer: Typical examples are areas where incorrect guidance leads to user decisions or disputes, such as legal, medical, and customer support documents. In these areas, trust in the service is determined by whether the user can directly check the evidence, rather than whether the answer is right or wrong.

items.prompt: What do users do when you have a source link?
items.answer: Instead of just believing the answer, users can go to the original text and check it for themselves. A source is not a device that forces belief, but a device that opens the way for verification. This perspective becomes important again at the end of the lesson.

items.prompt: Is the answer necessarily correct just because the source is attached?
items.answer: The fact that a source is attached only tells you which document this answer came from. Whether that document is up to date and accurate is another matter. In the following screens, we will see examples of why this difference is important.

screens.outro: Now let's see how Claude's Citations work with requests and responses.

screens.title: Structure of Claude Citations
screens.lead: The code below shows a request for a document block with quotes turned on, followed by a text block in the response. Read the descriptions for each line number to determine which line in the request leads to which field in the response.

notes.note: The source of the document block. Only source data can be cited. Plain text documents are chunked into sentences, so the model cites a single sentence or a series of sentences.

The title is passed to the model, but is not the content to be quoted. The same goes for the context field. The metadata of the document is placed in these two fields, and the content to be cited is placed in data.

Setting citations.enabled to true turns on citations. Within a request, it must be turned on for all documents or turned off for all. If this line is omitted, the response will not have a citations field.
The response is divided into text blocks by argument, and each block is accompanied by an array of citations. This means that each answer sentence is followed by a location of evidence.

char_location is the citation format for plain text documents. cited_text is a passage taken from the original text, document_index is the document order in the request, if 0 is the first document. Letter positions are counted starting from 0 and do not include the ending position. For PDFs, page numbers start from 1, and for custom content, block numbers start from 0.

Currently only text citations are supported, image citations are not supported. So you can't quote a scanned PDF where you can't extract the text. Turning on quoting slightly increases the number of input tokens due to the addition of system prompts and document chunking.

screens.outro: Now that I've seen the case for uploading documents directly, I'll compare how I forward my search results with sources to Gemini's grounding.

screens.title: search_result block and Google Search grounding
screens.lead: Select each tab to compare the structure of how to cite your own search results, Gemini's grounding, and generic answers.

tabs.label: search_result block
tabs.body:
A block of content that allows Claude to cite the results my search system finds. `type`, `source`, `title`, `content` are required. `source` can be a URL or an internal identifier such as `kb://article-1234`. `content` contains an array of text blocks and cannot contain images.

Results are communicated in two ways. Your custom tool can return it as a result of the call, or you can put it directly into the top-level content of the user's message. When you turn on `citations`, Claude will quote automatically without prompting, and all search results from a request must use the same settings.

tabs.label: Google Search grounding
tabs.body:
Grounding with Google Search connects Gemini to real-time web content and provides verifiable provenance. It increases factual accuracy, reduces model hallucinations, provides access to up-to-date information beyond the point of training, and increases user trust by showing the source.

When you turn on the `google_search` tool, the model analyzes the prompt, creates queries if necessary, runs a search, and synthesizes the results to create an answer. The text block in the response is appended with `annotations`, indicating the source URL, title, and position in the sentence as `url_citation`.

tabs.label: General answer with no basis
tabs.body:
If the model answers only with its own learned knowledge, without any citations or grounding, there will be no source field in the response. There is a sentence, but there are no clues as to which document it came from or what location it was based on.

In this case, the only way for users to check is to search elsewhere, and it is difficult for developers to trace the cause of incorrect answers. The biggest difference between the previous two methods is the presence or absence of this confirmation path.

screens.outro: Now that we've identified the differences between the three structures, let's contrast how the same answer appears to the user when it has evidence and when it doesn't.

screens.title: Differences in structure between answers with evidence and answers without evidence
screens.lead: Switch between the two states below and compare how the same answer changes when given evidence and no evidence.

visual.alt: Answers with evidence are linked to sentences, source titles, and original text locations, while answers without evidence are comparison pictures with only sentences.

states.label: There is evidence
states.body:
There is a link from the sentence to the source title and original text location. Users can see which part of the document this answer comes from and go to the original to check for themselves.

Citation notation is a device that allows users to go to the original text to check. So, we need to design how to show the source on the service screen. The verification path is completed by clicking on the source name to go to the original text location.

states.label: no basis
states.body:
There is only a sentence and no path to check. Users have to search separately to determine if the answer is correct, and it is difficult for developers to track where the error occurred.

The absence of a source field does not mean that the answer is wrong, but it does mean that there is no way to check if it is correct. In services where trust is important, the absence of this verification is itself a risk.

screens.outro: Now that we have identified the structural differences, we will explain the dangers hidden in citations with examples.

screens.title: Case Commentary: Reading Citations When the Source Document Is Wrong
screens.lead: The instructor will explain step by step the cases where outdated terms and conditions are cited. Select the arrows to the right to follow which fields in the citation block you are looking at and determining what to look for.

steps.title: situation
steps.body: Outdated terms and conditions were listed and cited in search results. The text of the response is: Refunds are available within 14 days, and the citations include `"document_title": "Refund Terms_2021"` and `"cited_text": "Refunds are requested within 14 days of purchase."`

steps.title: Step 1: cited_text matches answer
steps.body: First, read `cited_text` to see if it matches the answer. The answer and quote are the same: refunds can be made within 14 days. The model cited the document accurately. There are no issues with the model's citation ability.

steps.title: Step 2: Looks trustworthy with citations
steps.body: The answer seems more believable because there is a quotation attached. Users also feel grounded and more accepting. This effect of quotation actually increases misunderstanding in this case.

steps.title: Step 3: But the original text is outdated
steps.body: As 2021 by `document_title` shows, the cited document is an outdated version. The current policy is different. Users end up believing outdated, accurately quoted information and have false expectations.

steps.title: Step 4: Quotation is not a guarantee
steps.body: A citation only tells you that it comes from this document and does not guarantee that the document is correct. So the reason this answer is wrong is not the citation function but document management. Identifying where to look for the problem is key to diagnosis.

steps.title: Step 5: Response
steps.body: There are three responses: It manages the recency of the document being searched, displays the date or version in the source, and provides users with a path to check the original text. The service design reflects the fact that if the cited document is incorrect, the answer may also be incorrect.

screens.outro: Now that we've summarized the cases, let's look at the standards for determining source policies at the service level.

screens.title: Set source policy
screens.lead: By selecting and expanding each item, you can read the criteria and reasons for consideration when determining the source policy. Take a look at them one by one from the perspective of designing a service.

items.title: Decide which sources you allow
items.body: First, scope out sources you can trust, such as official documents and internal knowledge bases. A wider tolerance increases the quality of the search, but also increases the risk of citing outdated or inaccurate documents. Narrow the scope to suit the risk level of your service.

items.title: Add date and version to source
items.body: As in the previous example, old documents that are cited accurately can create misunderstandings. Showing the date and version in your sources allows users and developers to quickly determine whether the document is up to date. There is a way to include this information in the title or source of search_result.

items.title: Show the user a link to the original text
items.body: A citation is a device that allows users to check the original text. Clicking on the source name next to the answer will provide a link to the original source to make it easier to check. If there is no link, it is as if the citation function is not visible to the user.

items.title: Provide guidance on the risk of evidence errors and establish a reporting channel.
items.body: We inform users that even if there is a source, the evidence itself may be incorrect, and provide a path to report errors when they are discovered. Reported cases help us improve document management and search settings.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the standards, we will conclude by summarizing the key points.

screens.title: Key points and reflection
screens.lead: Review the key points of this lesson on one screen. Read the paragraph below and proceed to the summary screen.

paragraphs: Quotations are a means of verification, not a basis for trust. Claude's Citations, search_result block, and Gemini's Grounding with Google Search all link answers to sources, while citation blocks point to documents and locations.

However, if the cited document is incorrect, the answer may also be incorrect. A provenance policy is needed to manage the recency of documents, date sources, and allow users to check the original text.

right: Provides verifiable sources by linking to real-time web content
Turn on document-based citations by setting it in a document block.
It is a search result unit with source, title, and content.
checks.explain: citations.enabled is the citation option for the document block, search_result is a search results block with sources, and Google Search grounding provides sources via a web connection.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded.
checks.q:
A block of quotes from the response is below: What is the correct interpretation?
{"type": "char_location", "cited_text": "The sky is blue.", "document_index": 0, "start_char_index": 20, "end_char_index": 36}
options: Refers to pages 20 through 36 of the second document in the request.
This is the sentence starting from the 20th character counting from 0 to before the 36th character in the first document of the request.
The quoted phrase is a new sentence written by the model, so it is unrelated to the location of the original text.
Count letters starting from 1 and quote them, including the last letter.
checks.explain: document_index counts from 0, so 0 is the first document, and character position also counts from 0, not including the end. The sentences from 20 to 36 are relevant.

wrong.0: Page numbers are used in PDF citations, where char_location indicates the character location, and the index counts from 0.
wrong.2: cited_text is a passage taken from the original text, and the location field indicates its location in the original text.
wrong.3: Character positions are counted starting from 0 and do not include the ending index.

checks.incorrectFeedback: Unfortunately, this is not the correct answer.

glossary.def: This is a feature where Claude attaches the source location to answers based on documents.
This is a feature where Gemini answers and provides sources based on real-time web search results.
This is a content block that delivers my search results along with the source and title so Claude can cite them.
The job is to show the user which document the answer came from.
There is a risk that the cited document itself may be incorrect and the correctly cited answer may provide incorrect guidance.

misconceptions.myth: If there is a citation, the answer is correct.
misconceptions.fact: Citations only show which document the answer comes from. If the original text is old or incorrect, the answer may be wrong even if it is cited accurately.

misconceptions.myth: When you use grounding, hallucinations disappear.
misconceptions.fact: Grounding is the ability to reduce hallucinations by keeping you grounded in real sources. It can't be completely eliminated, so users still need a way to verify the source.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Quotation is not a basis for trust, but a means of confirmation.
Claude Citations, search_result block, and Google Search grounding link answers to sources.
If the supporting document is incorrect, the citation may be misleading.
Each service needs a provenance policy.
